svg.aria-label: What you write versus what I2AS does: you write a driver class, a Virtual Instrument class with declared readings and controls, a devices.yaml naming instruments and limits, and optionally a procedure that turns roles and parameters into plans; the fixed framework builds the Station from that config, snapshots its declarations into StationInfo, and renders them unchanged into GUI panels, the capability manifest and the MCP tool schemas an agent reads.

g.text: Setting up a station: what you write, what the framework builds, what the agent sees
1 · YOU WRITE — four things, per instrument and per experiment
2 · THE FRAMEWORK — fixed, same for every setup
3 · WHAT THE AGENT AND THE GUI SEE
Plain Python over VISA or serial. Only if yours is not shipped yet.
Knows nothing above it. A simulated twin lets the stack run without hardware.
The declaration. Every unit, sentence and class here is what the agent reads.
description="Temperature to ramp the controller to")})
@monitored is a reading with a unit; @control a typed action with a class.
Conformance tests refuse a VI that leaves any blank. Drivers are injected, not imported.
Which instruments this rack has, at which addresses, with which limits.
Limits are setup properties, so they live in yaml, not code. Copy a shipped config to start.
A recipe: names roles, not instruments; returns plans; never touches hardware.
Drop the file in i2as/procedures/. Any named BaseProcedure subclass is discovered at launch.
The one factory. Runs on the instrument thread, at launch:
2. imports each driver class, opens its address
3. imports each VI class, injects its drivers by role,
passes init_params — limits, coil constants, tolerances
4. registers every VI in the Station by its yaml name
5. an instrument that fails to connect is registered
offline, never aborts the build; the GUI offers reconnect
i2as --config my_setup · i2as-doctor validates the yaml first
The frozen declaration snapshot, built once per launch from
the VI classes and the yaml, with no instrument traffic:
units, action class) · every configured bound · UI groups
JSON-safe, so it crosses threads and processes unchanged.
The engine — deterministic, never edited per setup
Orchestrator (single writer, one tick loop, state machine)
Procedure base classes · the four shipped procedures
Data manager (one HDF5 file per run) · run queue
Session layer · agent gateway · permission matrix
GUI · MCP adapter · request spool · analysis worker
Polls the VIs, dispatches commands within the bounds,
answers every action with a verdict. Same code on every rack.
StationInfo is turned into three surfaces by code that adds
no words of its own: GUI panels, the capability manifest,
Conformance tests diff the three, so a GUI button and an
agent tool can never disagree about what the station can do.
At launch, every named BaseProcedure subclass found in
i2as/procedures/ goes into the catalog {class name → class}.
A run request names the class. build_procedure() resolves
each role against the Station, validates every param against
its ParamSpec and the setup limits, and refuses by name
if it cannot honour the run — at queue time, not an hour in.
The engine (above) pulls the built run from the queue and
dispatches its plans through the Station, within the bounds.
MCP tool, as the agent receives it from tools/list
One tool per (instrument, @control). Name = yaml key + "__" + method.
The agent reads the unit, the bound and the sentence you wrote. A call outside
the bound is refused by the schema before a command is built. Whether it may
call the tool at all is its role against the action class (gradual exposure).
Readings arrive the same way: temperature = 4.20 K, plus the sentence you wrote.
Capability manifest — "what can this system do?" as JSON
Every instrument, grouped as its VI declared, with readings, controls,
bounds and the metadata block from the yaml (role, manufacturer, model).
i2as-ctl manifest # no engine, no GUI, no bus traffic
Validated against a published JSON Schema; safe to hand to any client.
GUI panel — the physicist's view of the same declaration
group, order and labels from ui_groups; the tooltip is the same description
An LLM agent has no other description of your rack. The sentence on a
@monitored is how it knows what a number means; the unit on a ParamSpec
is how it knows 4.2 is kelvin, not amps; the bound in devices.yaml is the
wall it cannot walk through. Write them as you would for a new lab member.
Nothing between your file and the agent adds, edits or summarises a word.
Procedure, as the agent runs it
Your class name and ParamSpecs are the arguments; a role offers only this rack's VIs.
validate_run # "may I run this, how long?" — no dispatch
probe_run # a real, cheap run of the recipe first
Both are run_control: a session-role agent may start them, an observer may only validate.
you write it in YAML, per rack
amber text came from your VI class · blue text came from your devices.yaml · everything else is generated
